processing: Standard sheng pu-erh: sun-dried maocha from old trees, kept loose or pressed, with no ripe-style fermentation.
harvest_season: Not documented for this plot; spring old-tree leaf is the prized picking in the Yiwu area.
appearance_dry: As is typical of Yiwu old-tree tea, long dark-green strands with pale buds.
appearance_liquor: In young tea, typically clear gold.
taste_profile: Little is documented about this tea on its own. Guafengzhai tea, of which it is part, is described as wild and broad while keeping Yiwu's fragrance and softness.

brewing.notes: Treat it as strong Yiwu: near-boiling water and short early steeps, then let it run.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, like other sheng, as premium spring old-tree tea in small lots. Since Guafengzhai names attract Laotian leaf passed off as local, ask directly about provenance. Because Tea King is also a common label, check which place is meant.
description:
Chawangshu, tea king tree, is a name within Guafengzhai, the remote Yao village on the Laos border in the east of the Yiwu area. It is ranked among the finest names in Yiwu by people who follow the area closely.

The trouble is the name. Tea king trees are also described behind Luoshuidong, at Mansa and in the Dingjiazhai gardens near Wangong, so the words alone do not tell you the place. The label is only useful alongside the word Guafengzhai.

The tea is made by normal sheng methods. Little is documented about what sets this plot apart in the cup, so the nearest guide is Guafengzhai as a whole: stronger and wilder than most Yiwu, yet soft and fragrant.

Buy it the way you would buy any costly Guafengzhai: from someone who will say exactly where it was picked, and with some doubt about low prices.
history: Little is documented about this plot. Guafengzhai itself became known to tea drinkers only after 2007, when interest in single-mountain pu-erh grew. No date for the first use of the name as a tea label is recorded.
